title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text:
Some words are best understood not as isolated definitions but as small windows onto culture: the courtroom and the plea, the turned head of the latecomer, the discreet power of the hotel concierge, the crackling tannoy of a British railway station, and the reassuring tally of a final count. This masterclass treats each in turn.



Phonetics: /pliːd/.


From Old French plaidier (“to plead a case”), from Medieval Latin placitare, from Latin placitum (“a decision, decree, plea”), from placere (“to please, be agreeable”). The same root yields plea, please, pleasant, placid, and complacent — a family united by the idea of satisfaction and agreement.





To plead is to formally answer a charge or argue a case in court: * “The defendant pleaded not guilty.” * “She pleaded her case with quiet conviction.” * “He pleaded the Fifth” (US: declined to answer on grounds of self-incrimination). * “They pleaded insanity.”



To beg earnestly, or to make an impassioned appeal: * plead for + thing: “The prisoner pleaded for mercy.” * plead with + person: “She pleaded with him to stay.” * plead to + infinitive: “They pleaded to be released.” * plead ignorance: “He pleaded ignorance of the rules.”




[ Intensity of Entreaty ]

Ask ───► Request ───► Plead ───► Beg ───► Implore ───► Entreat ───► Beseech ───► Supplicate
(mild)    (polite)    (earnest)  (humble) (emotional)  (formal)     (literary)   (abject)



Word
Nuance




Plead
Earnest, often emotional; also legal.


Beg
Humble, desperate, or informal.


Implore
Deeply emotional; appeals to feeling.


Entreat
Formal; appeals to reason or goodwill.


Beseech
Literary; archaic gravity.


Supplicate
Formal/religious; abject humility.




Note: The standard past tense is pleaded; the form pled is common in American and Scottish usage.


Model Sentence: “The villagers pleaded with the council for more time, but the demolition order stood.”






Phonetics: /ˈleɪtˌkʌm.ər/.


A person who arrives late — to an event, a party, a meeting, or (by extension) a field or trend: * “Latecomers were asked to wait at the back.” * “The company was a latecomer to the smartphone market.”




Latecomer is neutral; late arrival is a slightly more formal synonym.
Johnny-come-lately is a disparaging term for someone who arrives or joins late, with the implication of inexperience or opportunism: “Some Johnny-come-lately startup is now claiming to have invented it.”
By analogy, newcomer emphasizes being new rather than late; latecomer emphasizes the timing.


Model Sentence: “As a latecomer to streaming, the studio had to spend heavily to catch up.”






Phonetics: BrE /ˈkɒn.si.ɛəʒ/, AmE /ˌkɒn.siˈɛrʒ/.


From French concierge, from Old French, probably from Vulgar Latin conservius (“fellow servant,” from con- “with” + servus “servant”). The word has carried two distinct roles for centuries.




In France and some European cities: the caretaker or janitor of an apartment building, who manages the entrance, keys, and building affairs — a position of surprising power.
In hotels worldwide: the guest-services specialist who arranges reservations, tickets, transport, and local recommendations — the embodiment of discreet, resourceful hospitality.





Concierge desk / concierge service: a dedicated assistance function in hotels, airports, and offices.
Concierge medicine: a premium model in which patients pay a retainer for rapid, personalized access to a physician.
Digital concierge: an AI or app-based assistant offering the same personalized service.


Model Sentence: “The concierge secured impossible tickets, a private car, and a corner table — all before breakfast.”






Phonetics: /ˈtæn.ɔɪ/.


Tannoy is a genericized trademark. The name was coined in 1926 by the Scottish company Tannoy Ltd., and is a blend of tantalum (a metal used in early components) + alloy. Like hoover, biro, and sellotape, the brand name passed into common usage in Britain.



In British English, tannoy denotes a public-address system and, by metonymy, an announcement made over it: * “They announced the delay over the tannoy.” * “The tannoy crackled into life.” * “I heard my name on the tannoy.”




British: tannoy (informal to neutral); PA system (formal).
American: PA system, intercom, public address, or loudspeaker — tannoy is not used.


Model Sentence: “A voice over the tannoy apologised for the delay and invited passengers to Platform 4.”






Phonetics: /ˈtæl.i/.


From Anglo-Norman tallie and Medieval Latin tallia (“a cutting, a tally”), from Latin talea (“a rod, stick, cutting”). The historical tally stick — a notched wooden stick split lengthwise so that debtor and creditor each held half — was the original receipt. The notches recorded the debt; matching the two halves proved authenticity — hence the modern sense of “corresponding” or “agreeing.”






“Keep a tally of every expense.”
“The final tally was 42 votes to 38.”
“The tally of casualties rose overnight.”





tally (up) + object (count): “They tallied the ballots by hand.”
tally with + noun (agree): “Her account does not tally with the evidence.”
“The numbers simply don’t tally.”






Keep a running tally
The final tally
Tally up the results
His story tallies with hers
Tally sheet (a record sheet)


Note: Do not confuse tally with tally-ho (an unrelated fox-hunting cry) or with tallywhacker (slang).


Model Sentence: “By midnight the scrutineers had tallied every ballot, and the final tally confirmed the recount.”







“The guest arrived at the hotel as a latecomer, flustered and drenched. The concierge, unruffled, arranged a new reservation and, over the tannoy-like paging system, summoned the porter. The guest pleaded for a room with a view; the concierge promised to tally the available upgrades and report back within the hour.”





1. Which word is a British genericized trademark for a public-address system? A) concierge B) tannoy C) tally D) latecomer
2. What is the literal origin of “tally”? A) A clock tower B) A notched counting stick C) A hotel register D) A courtroom plea
3. Which pair is etymologically related? A) plead and please B) tally and tall C) tannoy and tanner D) concierge and concert
4. What does “Johnny-come-lately” most closely mean? A) A punctual person B) A disparaging term for a latecomer or newcomer C) A loyal regular D) A hotel manager
5. In “her account does not tally with the evidence,” what does “tally” mean? A) To count B) To agree or correspond C) To argue D) To record



B. Tannoy is a genericized British trademark (TannOy = tantalum alloy) for a PA system.
B. A tally was originally a notched stick (from Latin talea, “cutting/rod”) used to record debts.
A. Plead and please both descend from Latin placere / placitum.
B. Johnny-come-lately is a pejorative for a late or opportunistic arrival.
B. Tally with means to agree or correspond.

To beg earnestly, or to make an impassioned appeal: * plead for + thing: “The prisoner pleaded for mercy.” * plead with + person: “She pleaded with him to stay.” * plead to + infinitive: “They pleaded to be released.” * plead ignorance: “He pleaded ignorance of the rules.”

Formal/religious; abject humility.




Note: The standard past tense is pleaded; the form pled is common in American and Scottish usage.


Model Sentence: “The villagers pleaded with the council for more time, but the demolition order stood.”

title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text:
Phonetics: /ˈleɪtˌkʌm.ər/.


A person who arrives late — to an event, a party, a meeting, or (by extension) a field or trend: * “Latecomers were asked to wait at the back.” * “The company was a latecomer to the smartphone market.”




Latecomer is neutral; late arrival is a slightly more formal synonym.
Johnny-come-lately is a disparaging term for someone who arrives or joins late, with the implication of inexperience or opportunism: “Some Johnny-come-lately startup is now claiming to have invented it.”
By analogy, newcomer emphasizes being new rather than late; latecomer emphasizes the timing.


Model Sentence: “As a latecomer to streaming, the studio had to spend heavily to catch up.”

title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text:
Phonetics: BrE /ˈkɒn.si.ɛəʒ/, AmE /ˌkɒn.siˈɛrʒ/.


From French concierge, from Old French, probably from Vulgar Latin conservius (“fellow servant,” from con- “with” + servus “servant”). The word has carried two distinct roles for centuries.




In France and some European cities: the caretaker or janitor of an apartment building, who manages the entrance, keys, and building affairs — a position of surprising power.
In hotels worldwide: the guest-services specialist who arranges reservations, tickets, transport, and local recommendations — the embodiment of discreet, resourceful hospitality.





Concierge desk / concierge service: a dedicated assistance function in hotels, airports, and offices.
Concierge medicine: a premium model in which patients pay a retainer for rapid, personalized access to a physician.
Digital concierge: an AI or app-based assistant offering the same personalized service.


Model Sentence: “The concierge secured impossible tickets, a private car, and a corner table — all before breakfast.”

title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text:
Phonetics: /ˈtæn.ɔɪ/.


Tannoy is a genericized trademark. The name was coined in 1926 by the Scottish company Tannoy Ltd., and is a blend of tantalum (a metal used in early components) + alloy. Like hoover, biro, and sellotape, the brand name passed into common usage in Britain.



In British English, tannoy denotes a public-address system and, by metonymy, an announcement made over it: * “They announced the delay over the tannoy.” * “The tannoy crackled into life.” * “I heard my name on the tannoy.”




British: tannoy (informal to neutral); PA system (formal).
American: PA system, intercom, public address, or loudspeaker — tannoy is not used.


Model Sentence: “A voice over the tannoy apologised for the delay and invited passengers to Platform 4.”

title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text:
Phonetics: /ˈtæl.i/.


From Anglo-Norman tallie and Medieval Latin tallia (“a cutting, a tally”), from Latin talea (“a rod, stick, cutting”). The historical tally stick — a notched wooden stick split lengthwise so that debtor and creditor each held half — was the original receipt. The notches recorded the debt; matching the two halves proved authenticity — hence the modern sense of “corresponding” or “agreeing.”






“Keep a tally of every expense.”
“The final tally was 42 votes to 38.”
“The tally of casualties rose overnight.”





tally (up) + object (count): “They tallied the ballots by hand.”
tally with + noun (agree): “Her account does not tally with the evidence.”
“The numbers simply don’t tally.”






Keep a running tally
The final tally
Tally up the results
His story tallies with hers
Tally sheet (a record sheet)


Note: Do not confuse tally with tally-ho (an unrelated fox-hunting cry) or with tallywhacker (slang).


Model Sentence: “By midnight the scrutineers had tallied every ballot, and the final tally confirmed the recount.”

title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text: “The guest arrived at the hotel as a latecomer, flustered and drenched. The concierge, unruffled, arranged a new reservation and, over the tannoy-like paging system, summoned the porter. The guest pleaded for a room with a view; the concierge promised to tally the available upgrades and report back within the hour.”

title: Words of Appeals and Public Spaces: ‘Plead For’, ‘Latecomer’, ‘Concierge’, ‘Tannoy’, and ‘Tally’
text:
1. Which word is a British genericized trademark for a public-address system? A) concierge B) tannoy C) tally D) latecomer
2. What is the literal origin of “tally”? A) A clock tower B) A notched counting stick C) A hotel register D) A courtroom plea
3. Which pair is etymologically related? A) plead and please B) tally and tall C) tannoy and tanner D) concierge and concert
4. What does “Johnny-come-lately” most closely mean? A) A punctual person B) A disparaging term for a latecomer or newcomer C) A loyal regular D) A hotel manager
5. In “her account does not tally with the evidence,” what does “tally” mean? A) To count B) To agree or correspond C) To argue D) To record



B. Tannoy is a genericized British trademark (TannOy = tantalum alloy) for a PA system.
B. A tally was originally a notched stick (from Latin talea, “cutting/rod”) used to record debts.
A. Plead and please both descend from Latin placere / placitum.
B. Johnny-come-lately is a pejorative for a late or opportunistic arrival.
B. Tally with means to agree or correspond.

title: Revenant: The Returning Dead and the Vocabulary of Return
text:
English has a great many words for things that return, but only one that names the dead who return in the flesh: revenant. The word is a direct borrowing from French, where it is nothing more exotic than the present participle of the verb revenir, “to come back.” A revenant, etymologically, is simply one who is coming back.
That plain origin is the key to everything interesting about the word. It is not a word about souls — that is ghost, spirit, specter. It is a word about return, and it belongs to a deep and productive Latin family built on venire, “to come.”
[ THE RETURN-ROOT FAMILY ]   Latin: venire = "to come"

  re-  (back)   + venire ──► revenire ──► revenir  ──► REVENANT
                            (to come back)  (French)     (one who returns)
                                                 └──────► revenue   (that which returns)

  ad-  (to)     + venire ──► advenire ──► advent / adventure
  con- (together)+ venire ──► convenire ──► convene / convention
  in-  (into)   + venire ──► invenire  ──► invent / inventory
  inter-(between)+ venire ──► intervenire ──► intervene
  prae- (before)+ venire ──► praevenire ──► prevent
  sub- (under)  + venire ──► subvenire ──► souvenir  (to come to mind)



Pronunciation: /ˈrɛv.ə.nənt/. Stress falls on the first syllable in English (unlike French, where it falls at the end). The final syllable is weak — REV-uh-nunt, not rev-uh-NANT.
Definition (noun): a person who has returned from the dead, especially one who returns in bodily form; more loosely, anyone who returns after a long absence.
Definition (adjective, archaic/literary): returning, coming back — “a revenant spirit.”

“The village believed the drowned man had become a revenant.”
“He came back into public life like a revenant from a discredited era.”
“The novel is haunted by revenants — the unquiet dead and the unwelcome past alike.”

Register: literary, historical, and folklore studies; in contemporary prose it often carries a deliberate archaizing or gothic flavour. It is the precise term where zombie would be anachronistic and ghost would be wrong.

The word’s distinctive claim: a revenant returns bodily. A ghost may be a breath of cold air; a revenant is a corpse that walks back through the door. That physicality is the semantic core.





Because venire (“to come”) is one of the most productive roots in the Latin inheritance, revenant sits inside a large etymological clan. Seeing it whole makes the word easier to fix in memory.









Latin
Prefix sense
French
English




revenire
re- “back”
revenir
revenant, revenue


advenire
ad- “to”
avenir
advent, adventure, avenue


convenire
con- “together”
convenir
convene, convention, covenant


invenire
in- “upon”
inventer
invent, invention, inventory


intervenire
inter- “between”
intervenir
intervene, intervention


praevenire
prae- “before”
prévenir
prevent, prevention


subvenire
sub- “up, under”
souvenir
souvenir, subvention


circumvenire
circum- “around”
circonvenir
circumvent


contravenire
contra- “against”
contrevenir
contravene


supervenire
super- “above”
survenir
supervene


eventus (from evenire)
“come out”
événement
event, eventual






Revenue is a cousin of revenant. Revenue descends from the past participle of revenir — literally “that which has returned,” i.e. income coming back to the one who is owed it. The same root that gives us a walking corpse gives us a tax term — a memorable illustration of how far a root can travel.
Souvenir is a cousin too. Subvenire meant “to come up (into the mind),” and French souvenir retains that sense of memory. A souvenir is a memory-object: something that comes back to you.


Going deeper: the ven- forms also surface in venue (a place to which people come), avenue (a way of coming to a place), and provenance/provenience (origin — where a thing comes from). The root runs through English like a road.






A word of caution about a word that looks like family:

Revert comes from Latin revertere = re- + vertere (“to turn”), not venire (“to come”). It means to turn back — to return to a former state, practice, or owner.
Reversion (noun): a return to a previous state; also, in law, the return of property to its original owner or the owner’s heirs (a reversionary interest).
Revertant (noun, genetics): an organism or cell that has reverted — a mutant that regains the wild-type phenotype by a second mutation.









Word
Root
Meaning




Revenant
venire “come”
One who comes back, especially from the dead


Revert
vertere “turn”
Turn back to a former state; return to a former owner


Revertant
vertere “turn”
A mutant that has reverted (genetics)


Reversion
vertere “turn”
The act of returning; a legal right of return




Usage trap — “revert back”: because revert already contains “back” in its re-, the phrase revert back is a redundancy that careful writers avoid. “The system reverted to its default” — not “reverted back to its default.” The same logic condemns return back, recur back, and reiterate again.





Revenant is a member of a crowded semantic field. English inherited words for the returning dead from at least five traditions — Germanic, Latin, Celtic, Slavic, and West African — and the resulting vocabulary preserves their distinct theologies.










Word
Etymology
Core sense




Ghost
Old English gāst (breath, spirit)
The apparition of a dead person; the soul after death


Spirit
Latin spiritus (breath)
The non-physical part of a person; also a ghost, and also vitality or mood


Specter / spectre
Latin spectrum (appearance, image)
A ghost, but especially one that frightens; figuratively, a threatening prospect (“the specter of famine”)


Phantom
Greek phantasma (appearance)
An apparition, real or imagined; frequently figurative (phantom limb, phantom load)


Apparition
Latin apparere (to appear)
A striking or unexpected appearance; the neutral, clinical term for a ghostly sighting


Wraith
Scots, of obscure origin
A ghost; in Scottish lore, sometimes the apparition of a living person, portending death


Shade
Old English sceadu (shadow)
The classical term for a ghost — the shadows of the dead in Hades; now literary (“the shades of the departed”)


Fetch
Old English fæcce
A double or apparition of a living person, often a death omen (Irish and English folklore)














Word
Etymology
Core sense




Revenant
French revenir
A corpse that returns and walks; the neutral, literary term


Zombie
Haitian Creole, from West African nzambi (god, spirit)
A reanimated corpse without will, in Vodou belief; in cinema, a ravenous horde member


Ghoul
Arabic ghūl
A demon that robs graves and feeds on corpses; later, a person morbidly fascinated by death


Lich
Old English līc (body, corpse)
Fantasy: an undead sorcerer whose soul is preserved outside the body (in a phylactery)


Draugr
Old Norse draugr
The Icelandic undead: a corpse that guards its grave-mound, grows in size, and must be physically destroyed


Wight
Old English wiht (creature, being)
Archaic “person”; in fantasy, the barrow-wight — a grave-haunting undead


Vampire
Slavonic (cf. Serbian vampir)
A revenant that leaves the grave to feed on the living; arguably Europe’s most famous revenant type


Mummy
Persian/Arabic mūmiyā (bitumen)
An embalmed body; in fiction, a deliberate, vengeful revenant


Reanimant
Latin re- + anima (soul)
Rare coinage for “one reanimated” — useful when you want the concept without the folklore














Word
Etymology
Core sense




Poltergeist
German poltern (to make noise) + Geist (ghost)
A noisy spirit that moves objects; the German borrowing is literal


Banshee
Irish bean sídhe (woman of the fairy mound)
A female spirit whose wail announces a death; not an apparition so much as an omen


Doppelgänger
German (double + goer)
An apparition of a living person; a double


Lemure
Latin lemures (restless ghosts)
In Roman belief, the unquiet dead of the household; the animal lemur is named after them


Wendigo
Algonquian
A cannibalistic spirit of the northern forests; not a revenant, but a hunger-spirit


Ghost light / corpse candle
—
Folkloric lights that precede or follow a death




Etymological footnote: ghoul, poltergeist, and doppelgänger are reminders that the undead lexicon is one of English’s most borrowed semantic fields. Where Germanic and Celtic terms mostly name the appearance (ghost, shade, fetch), Semitic, German, and Norse terms name the behaviour (grave-robbing, noise-making, walking).






This is the distinction most worth internalising, because careless writing blurs it.










Revenant
Zombie
Ghost




What returns
The body
The body
The soul


Will
Retains personal intent (often vengeful)
Usually none; driven by hunger or a controller
Retains personality and memory


Origin
European folklore: unquiet dead, excommunicated, oath-breakers
Haitian Vodou, then Hollywood
Universal


Register
Literary, historical, gothic
Popular, cinematic, figurative
Everyday, neutral


Figurative use
“a revenant of the past” — a person or idea returning after long absence
“zombie company,” “zombie idea” — something dead that keeps operating
“ghost of a chance,” “ghosting someone”




Revenant is the word for bodily return with purpose.
Zombie is the word for bodily return without will.
Ghost is the word for return without a body.







The revenant is a documented medieval belief, not merely a literary invention. The twelfth-century English chronicler William of Newburgh, in his Historia rerum Anglicarum, records several revenant episodes — most famously a man of Berwick who rose from the dead and terrorised his town until the villagers exhumed and burned the body, and the tale of a revenant haunting Melrose Abbey. These accounts treat the revenant as a physical, dangerous nuisance to be dealt with by consecrated ground, dismemberment, or fire — exactly the draugr-logic of the Norse sources.



The draugr of the Icelandic sagas is the North’s revenant: it guards its grave-mound, swells to monstrous size, and must be wrestled and beheaded. See Grettis saga (Glamr) and the Eyrbyggja saga (the restless Þórólfr, whose corpse continues to trouble the household until it is moved).




Cinema: The Revenant (2015) is a useful test case. The title is not about the undead: Hugh Glass is a revenant in the root sense — a man who comes back from near-death and from the wilderness. The film thereby recovers the word’s plain, non-supernatural meaning.
Games and fantasy: Magic: The Gathering has printed cards named Revenant; Dark Souls and Elder Scrolls use draugr; the term now proliferates in role-playing games as a category of corporeal undead.
Figurative journalism: “a revenant from the 1980s,” “the revenant of an old scandal” — applied to people, policies, and ideas that return unbidden.






Revenant has escaped the graveyard. Its figurative deployment is elegant and slightly ominous, and it is best used sparingly.








Usage
Example
Effect




A person returned
“A revenant from the pre-war cabinet.”
Suggests a figure who should have stayed buried


An idea returned
“The revenant of inflationary thinking.”
Frames an old doctrine as something undead


Adjectival (literary)
“a revenant figure in the doorway.”
Archaic colouring; a deliberate gothic note


Collective
“a country of revenants.”
Suggests a whole society of the unburied



Caution: because the word is uncommon, it lands hard. Where ghost or return would be plain, revenant supplies literary weight and a hint of menace — a good reason to use it once, deliberately, and never as decoration.




The most common errors with this word are spelling and look-alike confusion, not misuse.








Wrong
Right
Why




revenenet
revenant
A non-word; it fuses revenant with the -net of cabinet or internet. The ending is -ant, the French present-participle suffix.


revennant
revenant
French has revenir (one n); the doubling is a phantom.


revenent
revenant
-ent and -ant are both real suffixes, but this word takes -ant.


relevant (in this context)
revenant
The two are not interchangeable and not related.


reverent
revenant
Reverent = feeling reverence (from revereri, “to revere”). A reverent ghost is a polite one — a different word.


remnant
revenant
Remnant = a surviving fragment (from remanere, “to remain”). A different root and a different meaning.


reliant
revenant
Reliant = dependent (from religare, “to bind”).








Word
Root
Meaning




Revenant
venire — to come
One who returns (from the dead)


Relevant
levare — to raise
Bearing on the matter at hand


Reverent
vereri — to revere
Showing deep respect


Remnant
manere — to remain
A leftover fragment


Reliant
ligare — to bind
Depending on


Remanent
manere — to remain
Residual (archaic, technical)




Memory hook: a revenant comes back; a reverent admires; a relevant matters; a remnant is what’s left. The roots differ in the middle — and so does the meaning.







“William of Newburgh’s revenant was no ghost: witnesses insisted the man walked in the flesh, and the only remedy was fire. The saga’s draugr was its Norse cousin; the Haitian zombie its descendant without a will; and the cinema’s shambling horde its debased heir. Yet when the aging statesman returned to the chamber, journalists reached past all of them for the older, plainer word: a revenant from a buried decade.”





1. Etymologically, “revenant” means: A) one who is revered B) one who comes back C) one who remains D) one who is relevant
2. Which word shares the venire (“to come”) root with “revenant”? A) revert B) remnant C) revenue D) reverent
3. What most precisely distinguishes a revenant from a ghost? A) A revenant is friendly. B) A revenant returns in bodily form; a ghost is disembodied. C) A revenant cannot speak. D) There is no difference.
4. Which word describes a reanimated corpse without will? A) revenant B) specter C) zombie D) wraith
5. The Norse equivalent of the revenant, guarding its grave-mound in the sagas, is the: A) poltergeist B) banshee C) doppelgänger D) draugr
6. Which sentence uses the word correctly? A) The accountant was a revenant man who respected his elders. B) The village feared the drowned sailor, who returned as a revenant. C) She was revenant to the details of the contract. D) Only a revenant of the evidence survived the flood.
7. The phrase “revert back” is criticized because: A) Revert is informal B) Revert already contains the sense “back,” so back is redundant C) It belongs to genetics only D) Revert means “to come”



B. From French revenir, the present participle of “to come back.”
C. Revenue descends from the same revenir/venire root; revert and remnant use vertere and manere, and reverent uses vereri.
B. The revenant’s defining trait is bodily return; a ghost is a disembodied spirit.
C. The zombie is the corpse without autonomous will, in Vodou-derived and cinematic tradition.
D. The draugr is the Norse/Icelandic undead of the sagas.
B. Only B uses the word in its established sense. A confuses revenant with reverent; C confuses it with relevant; D confuses it with remnant.
B. Re- already signals return, so revert back is a redundancy (compare return back, recur back).







Recurrence and Resurfacing: ‘Recur’, ‘Resurface’, ‘Rear Its Head’ — the general vocabulary of things that come back, including recrudescence, resurgence, and relapse.
Lapse, Relapse, Elapse — the labi family of slipping and returning, and the medical sense of relapse.
Idioms of Coming to Pass and Happening — come to pass, come about, and other verbs of occurrence.
Setting Apart and Tearing Apart — the apart family of distinction and separation.

Old English līc (body, corpse)
Fantasy: an undead sorcerer whose soul is preserved outside the body (in a phylactery)

Old Norse draugr
The Icelandic undead: a corpse that guards its grave-mound, grows in size, and must be physically destroyed

Old English wiht (creature, being)
Archaic “person”; in fantasy, the barrow-wight — a grave-haunting undead

Slavonic (cf. Serbian vampir)
A revenant that leaves the grave to feed on the living; arguably Europe’s most famous revenant type

Persian/Arabic mūmiyā (bitumen)
An embalmed body; in fiction, a deliberate, vengeful revenant

Latin re- + anima (soul)
Rare coinage for “one reanimated” — useful when you want the concept without the folklore

German poltern (to make noise) + Geist (ghost)
A noisy spirit that moves objects; the German borrowing is literal

Irish bean sídhe (woman of the fairy mound)

German (double + goer)
An apparition of a living person; a double

Algonquian
A cannibalistic spirit of the northern forests; not a revenant, but a hunger-spirit

Where Germanic and Celtic terms mostly name the appearance (ghost, shade, fetch), Semitic, German, and Norse terms name the behaviour (grave-robbing, noise-making, walking).

title: Revenant: The Returning Dead and the Vocabulary of Return
text:
The revenant is a documented medieval belief, not merely a literary invention. The twelfth-century English chronicler William of Newburgh, in his Historia rerum Anglicarum, records several revenant episodes — most famously a man of Berwick who rose from the dead and terrorised his town until the villagers exhumed and burned the body, and the tale of a revenant haunting Melrose Abbey. These accounts treat the revenant as a physical, dangerous nuisance to be dealt with by consecrated ground, dismemberment, or fire — exactly the draugr-logic of the Norse sources.



The draugr of the Icelandic sagas is the North’s revenant: it guards its grave-mound, swells to monstrous size, and must be wrestled and beheaded. See Grettis saga (Glamr) and the Eyrbyggja saga (the restless Þórólfr, whose corpse continues to trouble the household until it is moved).




Cinema: The Revenant (2015) is a useful test case. The title is not about the undead: Hugh Glass is a revenant in the root sense — a man who comes back from near-death and from the wilderness. The film thereby recovers the word’s plain, non-supernatural meaning.
Games and fantasy: Magic: The Gathering has printed cards named Revenant; Dark Souls and Elder Scrolls use draugr; the term now proliferates in role-playing games as a category of corporeal undead.
Figurative journalism: “a revenant from the 1980s,” “the revenant of an old scandal” — applied to people, policies, and ideas that return unbidden.

title: Revenant: The Returning Dead and the Vocabulary of Return
text:
Revenant has escaped the graveyard. Its figurative deployment is elegant and slightly ominous, and it is best used sparingly.








Usage
Example
Effect




A person returned
“A revenant from the pre-war cabinet.”
Suggests a figure who should have stayed buried


An idea returned
“The revenant of inflationary thinking.”
Frames an old doctrine as something undead


Adjectival (literary)
“a revenant figure in the doorway.”
Archaic colouring; a deliberate gothic note


Collective
“a country of revenants.”
Suggests a whole society of the unburied



Caution: because the word is uncommon, it lands hard. Where ghost or return would be plain, revenant supplies literary weight and a hint of menace — a good reason to use it once, deliberately, and never as decoration.

text:
The most common errors with this word are spelling and look-alike confusion, not misuse.

Why

A non-word; it fuses revenant with the -net of cabinet or internet. The ending is -ant, the French present-participle suffix.

-ent and -ant are both real suffixes, but this word takes -ant.

title: Revenant: The Returning Dead and the Vocabulary of Return
text: “William of Newburgh’s revenant was no ghost: witnesses insisted the man walked in the flesh, and the only remedy was fire. The saga’s draugr was its Norse cousin; the Haitian zombie its descendant without a will; and the cinema’s shambling horde its debased heir. Yet when the aging statesman returned to the chamber, journalists reached past all of them for the older, plainer word: a revenant from a buried decade.”

B. From French revenir, the present participle of “to come back.”

B. Only B uses the word in its established sense. A confuses revenant with reverent; C confuses it with relevant; D confuses it with remnant.
B. Re- already signals return, so revert back is a redundancy (compare return back, recur back).

title: The Lapse Family: ‘Lapse’, ‘Lapse Into’, ‘Relapse’, ‘Elapse’, and the Semantics of Sliding
text:
The English word family built on lapse descends from a single, vivid Latin verb: lābī, meaning “to slip, glide, slide, or fall.” The physical image — something quietly sliding out of position — generates an entire conceptual field: memory that slips, time that slides away, illness that slides back, and structures that fall down.
Where the clināre family (incline, decline, recline) is about tilting, the lābī family is about slipping — a gentler, more insidious kind of falling.
                        [ THE lābī FAMILY ]

   Latin lābī (to slip, glide, fall)
        │
        ├── lapse    (a slip; a falling-away from a standard)
        ├── relapse  (re- "back" + lābī → to slip back into illness)
        ├── elapse   (e- "out" + lābī → of time: to slip away)
        ├── collapse (com- "together" + lābī → to fall down together)
        ├── prolapse (prō- "forward" + lābī → to slip forward, out of place)
        └── lapsus   (a slip: lapsus linguae = slip of the tongue)



Phonetics: /læps/.


From Latin lapsus (“a slipping, a fall”), the past participle of lābī.





A lapse is a momentary breakdown in attention, memory, judgment, or conduct — a blemish in an otherwise continuous standard:

“A lapse in concentration cost him the match.”
“She apologised for her lapse in judgment.”
“A momentary lapse of memory.”




A lapse can also mean the interval between two events — a passage of time: * “After a lapse of ten years, he returned to his hometown.” * “A time lapse video compresses hours into seconds.”





A mistake is a generic inaccuracy.
An error may be systematic or technical.
A lapse implies a temporary suspension of an otherwise maintained standard — a gap, not a wrong answer. It is the word of moral and cognitive slipping.


Model Sentence: “The encryption was unbroken; the breach began with a single, human lapse — a password written on a sticky note.”











“He lapsed into old habits.”
“Her attention lapsed during the lecture.”




Legal, insurance, and subscription register — when something is not renewed, it simply slips away: * “My gym membership lapsed last month.” * “The insurance policy will lapse if the premium is unpaid.” * “The lease lapsed and the tenant lost the right of renewal.”

Note: For time itself, English prefers the dedicated verb elapse (see §4), though lapse can be used of time in formal prose.







The prepositional construction lapse into (+ noun) is one of the most evocative in English. It means to gradually and often involuntarily pass into a state — usually a negative, passive, or unconscious one:

“The patient lapsed into a coma.”
“A hush fell, and the room lapsed into silence.”
“After the divorce, he lapsed into depression.”
“The conversation lapsed into small talk.”










Expression
Connotation




Lapse into
Gradual, passive, often involuntary slide into a state.


Fall into
More abrupt; can also mean to acquire a habit (“fell into a routine”).


Relapse into
A return to a previous bad state after recovery.




Model Sentence: “As the last witness left the stand, the courtroom lapsed into a heavy, exhausted silence.”






Phonetics: /rɪˈlæps/ (verb), /ˈriːlæps/ (noun — note the stress shift).


Latin re- (“back, again”) + lābī (“to slip”) + the -apse reflex. Literally: “to slip back” — to slide back into a condition one had escaped.



Relapse describes the return of a disease, addiction, or bad condition after a period of improvement. It is predominantly medical and psychological:

Verb: “He relapsed into drinking after two years of sobriety.”
Noun: “She suffered a relapse and returned to hospital.”




[ The Arc of Illness and Recovery ]

  Onset ───► Treatment ───► Remission ───► RELAPSE ───► Recovery / Chronicity
                              (improved)    (slipped back)




Relapse implies a return to a previous bad state after an apparent improvement.
Recurrence is a more clinical, neutral term for a condition happening again, without the moral or behavioural weight of relapse.


Model Sentence: “The oncologist warned that a relapse was possible within five years, and urged vigilant monitoring.”






Phonetics: /ɪˈlæps/.


Latin e-/ex- (“out of, away”) + lābī. Literally: “to slip away.”



Elapse is used exclusively of time. It is formal and slightly literary, and it has no other sense:

“Three hours elapsed before the rescue team arrived.”
“A decade elapsed between the two discoveries.”





Elapse = (of time) to pass by. Intransitive, time-only, no negative connotation.
Lapse = to fail / expire / slide into a state.


❌ “Two years lapsed before he returned.” (possible but unusual) ✅ “Two years elapsed before he returned.”


Model Sentence: “Only minutes elapsed between the alarm and the evacuation, yet they felt like hours.”








Latin com- (“together”) + lābī → “to fall down together.” A physical, structural, or systemic sudden fall: * “The bridge collapsed under the weight.” * “The talks collapsed after three days.” * “He suffered a collapse from exhaustion.”



Latin prō- (“forward”) + lābī → “to slip forward.” A medical term in which an organ slips out of its normal position: * “Uterine prolapse,” “rectal prolapse,” “mitral valve prolapse.”



Describes someone or something that has slipped away from a former state — no longer active, practicing, or valid: * “A lapsed subscription.” * “A lapsed Catholic.” * “A lapsed member of the society.”



A formal term for a slip: * “A lapsus linguae” — a slip of the tongue. * “A lapsus calami” — a slip of the pen.













Word
Pattern
Example




Lapse (v.)
lapse into + state
“lapse into silence”


Lapse (n.)
a lapse in + quality; a lapse of + time
“a lapse in judgment; a lapse of years”


Relapse (v.)
relapse into + state
“relapse into addiction”


Relapse (n.)
suffer / have a relapse
“a relapse of the disease”


Elapse
(time) elapse — intransitive
“hours elapsed”


Collapse
collapse under / into / from
“collapse from exhaustion”


Lapsed
attributive adjective
“a lapsed member”

















Word
Part of Speech
Core Meaning
Temporal Frame
Register




Lapse
Noun
A slip or interval
Momentary / interval
Neutral


Lapse
Verb
Fail, expire, slide into
Transition
Neutral/formal


Relapse
Noun/Verb
Return to illness or vice
Regression
Medical/psych


Elapse
Verb
(Time) to pass
Duration
Formal


Collapse
Noun/Verb
Sudden structural fall
Sudden
Neutral/formal


Prolapse
Noun/Verb
Organ slips out of place
Displacement
Medical


Lapsed
Adjective
No longer active
State
Neutral/formal








“After a brief lapse in vigilance, the security team watched the situation lapse into chaos. Two hours elapsed before reinforcements arrived. The chief, lapsed into silence, feared a full relapse of the crisis; and when the eastern tower collapsed, it seemed the whole operation might lapse entirely.”





1. Which verb is used exclusively of time? A) lapse B) relapse C) elapse D) collapse
2. What does “lapse into silence” mean? A) To break the silence abruptly B) To gradually pass into a state of silence C) To refuse to speak D) To expire, as of a contract
3. What is the key difference between lapse and relapse? A) There is none. B) Relapse implies returning to a previous bad state after improvement. C) Lapse is always medical. D) Relapse is used only of time.
4. A “lapsed Catholic” is someone who: A) has no religion at all. B) has ceased practicing the faith. C) has just converted. D) attends church daily.
5. Which sentence uses the correct word? A) Three years relapsed before they met again. B) Three years elapsed before they met again. C) Three years lapsed into before they met again. D) Three years collapsed before they met again.



C. Elapse is used exclusively of the passage of time.
B. Lapse into means to slide gradually into a state (here, silence).
B. Relapse denotes a slip back into a prior condition after improvement.
B. Lapsed describes someone who has fallen away from active practice.
B. Elapsed is the correct verb for the passage of time.

title: Conversational Architecture: High-Fidelity Active Listening
text:
Most people do not listen; they simply reload. While the other person speaks, they are rehearsing their rebuttal or waiting for a polite pause to interject their own story.
True active listening is an active information-gathering discipline. It requires suppressing your internal ego dialogue and attending strictly to the semantic and emotional signals being transmitted.

title: Conversational Architecture: High-Fidelity Active Listening
text:
The Three Tiers of Listening

Level 1: Internal Listening: You hear the words, but your focus is on what they mean to you (e.g., “How does this affect my weekend?”).
Level 2: Focused Listening: Your attention is locked onto the speaker’s words, cadence, tone, and body language.
Level 3: Global Listening: You perceive the entire context: the unspoken tensions in the room, what is deliberately not being said, and the latent psychological currents.

title: Conversational Architecture: High-Fidelity Active Listening
text:
Tactical Techniques

Dynamic Mirroring: Repeating the last 1 to 3 critical words spoken with an inquisitive upward inflection. This triggers an instinctive biological urge in the speaker to elaborate.
Paraphrasing Latent Meaning: “If I understand correctly, the primary friction point isn’t the deadline itself, but the uncertainty in API stability?”
Comfort with Silence: The power of the 4-second pause. When you remain silent after someone finishes speaking, they will frequently fill the void with their most honest, vulnerable, and informative disclosures.

title: Effective Communication & Discourse
text:
Communication is not merely transmitting data; it is managing cognitive load in the mind of the listener or reader. Whether drafting an engineering specification, leading an asynchronous team, or addressing an auditorium, clarity is achieved through structure, brevity, and empathetic perspective-taking.

title: The Toulmin Model of Argumentation
text: While classical Aristotelian syllogisms (All men are mortal…) provide mathematical elegance, practical human debate deals with probabilistic evidence and contingent reality. British philosopher Stephen Toulmin developed a practical model that mirrors how robust arguments function in law, academia, and policy.

title: The Toulmin Model of Argumentation
section: The Six Elements of the Toulmin Model
text:
The Six Elements of the Toulmin Model
   [ Grounds / Data ] ────────( Warrant )────────> [ Claim ]
                             │                      ▲
                         ( Backing )                │
                                              ( Qualifier )
                                                    ▲
                                                    │
                                              ( Rebuttal )

Claim: The assertion you are asking the audience to accept (“Our distributed system requires idempotent retry semantics”).
Grounds (Data / Evidence): The empirical facts or data verifying the assertion (“Network partition metrics show 2.4% transient packet drops leading to duplicate billing events”).
Warrant: The underlying principle or logical bridge connecting the grounds to the claim (“Duplicate billing causes immediate customer churn and financial audit failures”).
Backing: Additional evidence validating the warrant (“Financial industry studies demonstrate a 40% churn rate after incorrect billing charges”).
Qualifier: The scope or degree of certainty (“Under heavy cross-region network congestion, almost certainly…”).
Rebuttal / Counter-Condition: Explicitly addressing the conditions under which the claim would not hold (“Unless transactions are secured via a strictly local atomic commit protocol”).

By systematically filling in all six slots, you protect your thesis from trivial dismissal and expose hidden assumptions in your opponent’s case.

title: Debating, Dialectic & Formal Logic
text:
Debate is the crucible in which ideas are stress-tested against rigorous scrutiny. Effective debaters do not rely on oratorical bluster; they understand the structural architecture of deductive and inductive arguments, the Toulmin model of validation, and the precise mechanics of refutation.



Argument Construction: The Toulmin structural model (Claim, Grounds, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal).
Catalog of Fallacies: Identifying and deconstructing cognitive and logical fallacies in real-time.
Refutation & Poise: Cross-examination tactics, time management, and turning opponent arguments to your advantage.

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text: Every English sentence is an assemblage of words acting in coordinated syntactic roles. Traditional English grammar identifies eight primary parts of speech. Rather than memorizing dictionary labels, one must understand their functional behavior in context.

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text: Every English sentence is an assemblage of words acting in coordinated syntactic roles. Traditional English grammar identifies eight primary parts of speech. Rather than memorizing dictionary labels, one must understand their functional behavior in context.

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text:
1. Nouns (\(N\)) and Pronouns (\(Pro\))

Nouns: Semantic anchors designating entities (concrete, abstract, collective, proper).
Pronouns: Deictic substitutions preventing repetitive strain. Critical distinctions include subjective (I, he, they), objective (me, him, them), possessive (mine, his, theirs), and reflexive (myself, themselves).

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text:
2. Verbs (\(V\))
The engine of the sentence. Verbs convey action, occurrence, or state of being (copular/linking verbs). * Transitive: Require a direct object (\(S-V-O\): “She analyzed the dataset”). * Intransitive: Complete without an object (\(S-V\): “The engine stalled”). * Linking: Connect a subject to a subject complement (\(S-V-C\): “The argument remains sound”).

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text:
3. Adjectives (\(Adj\)) and Adverbs (\(Adv\))

Adjectives: Modify nominal elements, answering which one, what kind, or how many.
Adverbs: Modify verbs, adjectives, or entire clauses, answering how, when, where, or to what degree.

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text:
4. Prepositions (\(Prep\))
Relational connectors establishing spatial, temporal, or logical vectors between nominal phrases and the rest of the clause (in, on, through, beyond, despite).

See also: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions and Dependent Prepositions & Collocations.

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text:
5. Conjunctions (\(Conj\))
Structural joints binding words, phrases, or clauses: * Coordinating (FANBOYS): For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So (joins syntactically equivalent units). * Subordinating: Although, because, since, while, unless (creates dependent clauses). * Correlative: Paired conjunctions (neither/nor, either/or, not only/but also).

title: The Eight Parts of Speech: Functional Anatomy of English
text:
6. Interjections (\(Int\))
Autonomous affective exclamations syntactically independent of the sentence.

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
Prepositions are short, unassuming words — at, in, on, of, to, by, for, with — yet they carry an enormous share of a sentence’s meaning. There are only about 150 of them, making prepositions a closed class: new ones are rarely coined, and the same handful recur with bewildering frequency. They are also the most idiomatic words in English. Logic alone will not tell you why we say good at but interested in, depend on but consist of. Prepositions must be learned as collocations as much as rules.
A preposition links a noun, pronoun, or gerund (its object) to another part of the sentence, expressing a relationship of place, time, direction, cause, manner, agency, or possession.

There are only about 150 of them, making prepositions a closed class: new ones are rarely coined, and the same handful recur with bewildering frequency. They are also the most idiomatic words in English. Logic alone will not tell you why we say good at but interested in, depend on but consist of. Prepositions must be learned as collocations as much as rules.
A preposition links a noun, pronoun, or gerund (its object) to another part of the sentence, expressing a relationship of place, time, direction, cause, manner, agency, or possession.

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
1. The Four Formal Categories

A. Simple (one-word) Prepositions
at  by  for  from  in  of  on  to  with  without  over  under
up  down  off  near  past  since  until  through  between  among


B. Compound (two-word) Prepositions
Formed by adding a prefix to a simple preposition:
into   onto   upon   within   without   throughout   alongside
amidst  amongst  toward  towards  outside  inside  notwithstanding


C. Complex (multi-word / phrasal) Prepositions
Fixed phrases functioning as a single preposition:
in front of     on behalf of     in spite of      because of
due to          owing to         apart from       according to
by means of     with regard to   in terms of      next to
out of          as for           except for       instead of
prior to        subsequent to    in addition to   with respect to


D. Double Prepositions
Two prepositions working together:
from behind   from under   from beneath   from among   until after   out of
“He emerged from behind the curtain.” / “She waited until after the ceremony.”

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
2. Prepositions of Place and Location

The at / in / on System
The three most important place prepositions form a system based on how we conceive of the location:








Preposition
Concept
Examples




at
A point or location seen abstractly
at the door, at the station, at the party, at 10 Downing Street


in
An enclosed space, area, or volume
in the box, in London, in the car, in the water


on
A surface; a line; public transport
on the table, on the wall, on the bus, on the third floor




Subtle difference: “I’ll meet you at the station” (a meeting point) vs. “I’ll wait in the station” (inside the building) vs. “I’m on the train” (aboard).



Other Spatial Prepositions







Preposition
Relationship




above / over
Higher than (over often implies covering or movement across)


below / under / underneath / beneath
Lower than (underneath emphasizes being directly beneath; beneath is literary)


between
In the space separating two things


among
Surrounded by three or more


beside / next to / by / near
At the side of; close to


behind / in front of
To the rear / to the front of


opposite / across from
Facing


along / around / past / beyond / through
Following a length, encircling, passing, further than, penetrating

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
3. Prepositions of Time

The at / on / in System








Preposition
Use
Examples




at
Clock times, points in the day, festivals
at 6 o’clock, at noon, at night, at Christmas


on
Days and dates
on Monday, on 4 July, on my birthday, on the weekend (AmE)


in
Months, years, seasons, longer periods, parts of the day
in July, in 2026, in winter, in the morning





Other Temporal Prepositions








Preposition
Meaning
Example




for
Duration
for three hours


since
From a past point until now
since 2020


during
Within a period (not its length)
during the film


until / till
Up to a point (continuation)
until midnight


by
No later than a deadline
by Friday


before / after
Earlier / later than
before dawn, after lunch


within
Inside a limit of time
within an hour


throughout
For the whole of a period
throughout the year


between … and
A span with two limits
between 9 and 5




Critical contrast — “by” vs. “until”: “Finish it by Friday” = deadline (finish at or before Friday). “Wait until Friday” = continue waiting up to Friday.

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
4. Prepositions of Movement and Direction
to      into     onto     toward(s)   through   across   along
around  past     over     under       up        down      out of
off     from     back to

“She walked to the door, through the hall, and out of the building.”
“The cat jumped onto the table and off again.”
He ran toward the exit, past the guards, and down the stairs.”*

Note the distinction between in/into (location vs. movement): “She is in the room” (location) vs. “She walked into the room” (movement).

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
5. Prepositions of Other Semantic Roles








Role
Prepositions
Example




Agent
by
“written by Orwell”


Instrument
with
“cut with a knife”


Cause / reason
because of, due to, owing to, on account of, thanks to, for
“cancelled due to rain”


Purpose
for, for the sake of
“a tool for cutting”


Manner / means
by, with, in, without
“travelled by train”


Possession / measure
of
“a cup of tea”


Topic / regard
about, on, of, regarding, concerning, over
“a book about Rome”


Concession
despite, in spite of, notwithstanding
“despite the storm”

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
6. Prepositional Phrases and Their Functions
A preposition plus its object forms a prepositional phrase, which can function as:

Adjectival (modifying a noun): “the man in the hat,” “a matter of principle.”
Adverbial (modifying a verb, adjective, or the whole clause): “She left in a hurry,” “famous for her wit.”

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
7. Prepositions vs. Particles vs. Adverbs
The same word can play different roles. Compare up:







Sentence
Function of up




“She climbed up the hill.”
Preposition (has object the hill)


“She looked up the word.”
Particle (part of phrasal verb; object the word)


“She looked up.”
Adverb (no object)



Test: A preposition is always followed by its object; a particle is bound to the verb and changes its meaning; an adverb is independent.

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
8. Grammatical Rules and Persistent Myths

Ending a sentence with a preposition is perfectly grammatical. English “strands” prepositions: “That’s the book I told you about.” The formal alternative (pied-piping) is “the book about which I told you,” which is appropriate in very formal prose but not required.
Prepositions govern gerunds, not infinitives: ✅ “interested in learning,” ❌ “interested in to learn.”
Use the object case after a preposition: ✅ “between you and me,” ❌ “between you and I.”
A preposition never takes a verb as its object (except in the gerund form).
Avoid unnecessary prepositions: ❌ “discuss about the plan” → ✅ “discuss the plan.”

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
9. Common Errors

❌ “I’ll meet you in the corner of the street.” → ✅ “on the corner” / “at the corner.” ❌ “I have been here since three hours.” → ✅ “for three hours.” ❌ “Finish it until Friday.” → ✅ “Finish it by Friday.” ❌ “Married with him.” → ✅ “Married to him.” ❌ “Different than” (AmE acceptable) → ✅ “Different from” (standard BrE) / “different to” (BrE informal).

title: The Complete Guide to English Prepositions: Types, Functions, and the at/in/on System
text:
10. Knowledge Check
1. Which sentence uses the correct preposition? A) I’ll meet you in the corner. B) I’ll meet you at the corner.
2. Choose the correct form: “She has lived here ___ 2015.” A) for B) since
3. When do we use “by” rather than “until”? A) To express a deadline (“finish by 5”). B) To express continuous waiting.
4. Which is the object case? A) between you and I B) between you and me
5. In “she looked up the word,” what is “up”? A) A preposition B) A particle C) A noun

Answer Key

B. At the corner treats the location as a point; in the corner suggests an enclosed inner corner.
B. Since marks a starting point continuing to now; for would require a duration (for ten years).
A. By marks a deadline; until marks continuation up to a point.
B. Prepositions take the object case (me).
B. Up is a particle forming the phrasal verb look up.

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text: The future continuous describes an action that will be in progress at a particular moment in the future. It differs from the simple future in the same way the past continuous differs from the past simple: it foregrounds the process unfolding rather than the event or result.

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text: The future continuous describes an action that will be in progress at a particular moment in the future. It differs from the simple future in the same way the past continuous differs from the past simple: it foregrounds the process unfolding rather than the event or result.

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Formation
Subject + will be + present participle (-ing)










Affirmative
Negative
Interrogative




All subjects
She will be working
She won’t be working
Will she be working?

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Core Uses

1. Action in Progress at a Future Moment

“This time tomorrow I will be flying to Tokyo.”
“At midnight they will still be dancing.”



2. Predicting or Describing Future States

“Don’t call at eight — we will be having dinner then.”
“The city will be celebrating its centenary all week.”



3. Polite Inquiries About Someone’s Plans
This is one of the most useful functions — asking about plans without imposing: * “Will you be using the car this evening?” * “Will you be attending the conference?”


4. Assumptions About the Present (a special idiom)
Will be + -ing can describe what is probably happening right now: * “Don’t worry — she will be waiting for us at the gate.” (= she is probably waiting now) * “He will be sleeping; it’s three in the morning.”

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Future Continuous vs. Future Simple







Future Continuous
Future Simple




Action in progress at a future time
A future event, decision, or prediction


“I will be seeing her tomorrow.” (arranged/in progress)
“I will see her tomorrow.” (intention/arrangement)


Neutral description of a future state
Volition, promise, or decision


“I’ll be working late.” (fact)
“I’ll work late.” (resolve)




Subtle difference: “I’ll be seeing him at the meeting” simply states what will occur; “I’ll see him at the meeting” can imply a decision or promise to do something (e.g., to speak to him).

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Nuances

No imposition: The future continuous softens requests and questions — “Will you be using this?” feels less demanding than “Are you going to use this?”
Parallel future actions: Two continuous actions can run side by side: “While I will be presenting, the team will be answering questions online.”
Stative verbs: As always, stative verbs avoid the continuous: ❌ “I will be knowing the result.” → ✅ “I will know the result.”

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Common Errors

❌ “I will be know the answer.” → ✅ “I will know the answer.” ❌ “I will be working here since 2020.” → ✅ “I will have been working here for five years.” (duration to a future point) ❌ “Will you use the car tonight?” (can sound like a request for permission) → ✅ “Will you be using the car tonight?” (neutral inquiry)

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Model Sentences

“By the time you read this, the interns will be presenting their findings, the partners will be arguing over the budget, and I will be sitting quietly in the back, taking notes.”

title: The Future Continuous Tense: Actions in Progress at a Future Time
text:
Knowledge Check
1. Which sentence best asks neutrally about someone’s plans? A) Will you use the car? B) Will you be using the car?
2. “Don’t call at seven — we ___ dinner.” A) will have B) will be having
3. Which is the correct assumption about the present? A) She will be waiting at the gate now. B) She will wait at the gate now.

Answer Key

B. The future continuous is the neutral, non-imposing inquiry.
B. An action in progress at a future moment takes the future continuous.
A. Will be + -ing can express a present assumption.

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text: The future perfect expresses an action that will be completed before a specified future point. It is the mirror image of the past perfect: where the past perfect looks backwards from a past moment, the future perfect looks backwards from a future moment. It answers the question “Will it be done by then?”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text: The future perfect expresses an action that will be completed before a specified future point. It is the mirror image of the past perfect: where the past perfect looks backwards from a past moment, the future perfect looks backwards from a future moment. It answers the question “Will it be done by then?”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Formation
Subject + will have + past participle (V3)










Affirmative
Negative
Interrogative




All subjects
She will have finished
She won’t have finished
Will she have finished?

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Core Uses

1. Completion Before a Future Deadline
Usually with by, by the time, before: * “By next June I will have graduated.” * “By the time you arrive, we will have eaten.”


2. Duration Ending at a Future Point
The future perfect can summarize a span completed by a future time: * “By 2030 she will have worked here for twenty years.”


3. Assumptions About the Past
A distinctive idiom: will have + V3 can express a confident deduction about something probably already done: * “Don’t worry — they will have received the message by now.” (= I assume they have received it) * “The plane will have landed an hour ago.”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Future Perfect vs. Future Simple







Future Perfect
Future Simple




Completed before a future point
A future event or decision


“I will have written the report by Friday.”
“I will write the report on Friday.”


Emphasizes completion/deadline
Emphasizes the action itself


“They will have left by the time we arrive.”
“They will leave at noon.”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
section: Future Perfect vs. Future Perfect Continuous
text:
Future Perfect vs. Future Perfect Continuous







Future Perfect
Future Perfect Continuous




Result / completion by a future point
Duration up to a future point


“By May I will have built the deck.”
“In May I will have been building the deck for two months.”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Nuances

With by: By + future time is the archetypal future perfect marker: “I will have submitted the thesis by September.”
“By then”: “They’re slow. They won’t have arrived by then.”
Stative verbs: With stative verbs, use the future perfect simple: “By next year I will have known her for a decade.”
Rare in casual speech: The future perfect is more common in formal, academic, and business registers.

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Common Errors

❌ “By next week I will finish it.” (fails to convey completion before the deadline) → ✅ “By next week I will have finished it.” ❌ “I will have went.” → ✅ “I will have gone.” (past participle) ❌ “By the time she comes, I will finish.” → ✅ “By the time she comes, I will have finished.”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Model Sentences

“By the time the audit concludes, the firm will have spent six million dollars on compliance, will have hired two hundred analysts, and, the partners hope, will have restored the regulator’s confidence.”

title: The Future Perfect Tense: Completion Before a Future Deadline
text:
Knowledge Check
1. Choose the correct sentence: A) By Friday I will finish the essay. B) By Friday I will have finished the essay.
2. What does “They will have received it by now” express? A) A future completion B) An assumption about the past
3. “By 2040, scientists ___ a cure.” A) will find B) will have found

Answer Key

B. By + future time signals completion before that point, requiring the future perfect.
B. Will have + V3 here expresses a confident deduction about the present/past.
B. The deadline (by 2040) requires the future perfect.

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text: The past continuous describes an action that was in progress at a particular moment in the past. It provides the atmospheric backdrop against which the past simple’s sharp events unfold. If the past simple is a series of snapshots, the past continuous is the film running between them.

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text: The past continuous describes an action that was in progress at a particular moment in the past. It provides the atmospheric backdrop against which the past simple’s sharp events unfold. If the past simple is a series of snapshots, the past continuous is the film running between them.

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Formation
Subject + was/were + present participle (-ing)










Affirmative
Negative
Interrogative




I / he / she / it
She was reading
She wasn’t reading
Was she reading?


you / we / they
They were reading
They weren’t reading
Were they reading?

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Core Uses

1. Action in Progress at a Past Moment

“At 8 p.m. yesterday I was watching the match.”
“This time last year we were sailing in Greece.”



2. Interrupted Action (Past Continuous + Past Simple)
The continuous action is interrupted by a sudden event: * “I was cooking dinner when the phone rang.” * “They were driving home when it started to snow.”


3. Simultaneous Actions

“She was cooking while he was cleaning.”
“While I was studying, my sister was watching TV.”



4. Background Scene in Narrative

“The sun was setting and birds were singing as the travellers reached the summit.”



5. Repeated, Often Annoying Past Habits
With always, constantly, forever: * “He was always losing his glasses.” * “They were constantly arguing about money.”


6. Polite or Tentative Requests (especially wondering, hoping)

“I was wondering if you could help me.”

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
section: Future in the Past: “Was/Were Going To”
text:
Future in the Past: “Was/Were Going To”
The past continuous of go expresses an intention or plan that existed in the past — often one that was not fulfilled: * “I was going to call you, but I lost my phone.” * “She was going to study medicine, but she chose law instead.”

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Past Continuous vs. Past Simple







Past Continuous
Past Simple




Action in progress
Completed action


“I was reading when he arrived.”
“I read the book last week.”


Background / scene-setting
Foreground / main events


“It was raining heavily.”
“I left the house at dawn.”


Not necessarily finished
Definitively finished




Combined pattern: “While I was walking home (continuous background), I saw an accident (sudden event).”

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Nuances

Interruption vs. overlap: If two actions simply coincide, both may be continuous (“We were talking while the rain was pouring”); if one interrupts the other, the interrupter takes the past simple.
Emotional colour: The continuous can imply a process that had not yet reached completion — “I was writing a novel” (and may never have finished it).
With stative verbs: As with all continuous forms, stative verbs are avoided: ❌ “I was knowing the answer.” → ✅ “I knew the answer.”

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Common Errors

❌ “When the phone rang, I cooked dinner.” → ✅ “When the phone rang, I was cooking dinner.” (the longer action is continuous) ❌ “I was knowing him well.” → ✅ “I knew him well.” ❌ “She was study when I called.” → ✅ “She was studying when I called.”

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Model Sentences

“While the orchestra was tuning and the audience was finding its seats, a lone violinist stepped forward and began to play — and the whole hall fell silent.”

title: The Past Continuous Tense: Setting the Scene
text:
Knowledge Check
1. Which sentence correctly shows an interruption? A) I cooked when she arrived. B) I was cooking when she arrived.
2. What does “I was going to call you” imply? A) I called you. B) I intended to call but perhaps did not.
3. Choose the correct form: “They ___ (play) football when it started to rain.” A) played B) were playing

Answer Key

B. The interrupted (longer) action takes the past continuous.
B. Was going to expresses a past intention, often unfulfilled.
B. The action in progress at the moment of interruption is continuous.

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text: The past perfect — “the past of the past” — locates an action before another past action or moment. It provides the essential sequencing that allows English to distinguish what happened first from what happened next. Without it, past narratives become temporally ambiguous.

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text: The past perfect — “the past of the past” — locates an action before another past action or moment. It provides the essential sequencing that allows English to distinguish what happened first from what happened next. Without it, past narratives become temporally ambiguous.

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Formation
Subject + had + past participle (V3)










Affirmative
Negative
Interrogative




All subjects
They had left
They had not (hadn’t) left
Had they left?



Had is invariable for all subjects.

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Core Uses

1. An Earlier Action Before Another Past Action

“When I arrived at the station, the train had already left.”
“She had finished the report before the meeting began.”



2. Sequencing with Time Markers
Common with before, after, by the time, already, just, never, once: * “By the time we got there, the film had started.” * “He had never seen snow until that winter.”


3. Reported (Indirect) Speech Backshift

Direct: “I have finished,” she said.
Reported: She said she had finished.
Direct: “We saw him yesterday.”
Reported: They said they had seen him the day before.



4. The Third Conditional (Unreal Past)

“If I had known the truth, I would have acted differently.”
“If she had studied, she would have passed.”



5. Explanations of Past States
The past perfect can explain the cause of a past situation: * “He was exhausted because he hadn’t slept for two days.”

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Past Perfect vs. Past Simple
The past perfect is only necessary when the order of events would otherwise be unclear. With before and after, the sequence is already explicit, so the past simple is often acceptable — though the past perfect adds clarity and emphasis.







Past Perfect (earlier event)
Past Simple (later event)




“The train had left when I arrived.”
“I arrived after the train left.”


“She had written the letter before he came.”
“She wrote the letter, then he came.”




❌ “When I arrived, the train left.” (implies the train left after you arrived) ✅ “When I arrived, the train had left.” (the train left before you arrived)

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Nuances

Optional past perfect: With before/after the sequence is clear, so “After he left, we talked” is fine — but “After he had left, we talked” is more precise.
“Had been to” vs. “had gone to”: “She had been to Paris” = she had visited and returned; “She had gone to Paris” = she had left for Paris.
Inversion for drama: “No sooner had I sat down than the phone rang.”
Emphasis on regret: The past perfect often carries a tone of missed opportunity: “I wish I had studied harder.”

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Common Errors

❌ “When I arrived, he already left.” → ✅ “When I arrived, he had already left.” ❌ “If I would have known…” → ✅ “If I had known…” ❌ “She said she has finished.” → ✅ “She said she had finished.”

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Model Sentences

“By the time the rescuers reached the cabin, the storm had passed, the fire had gone out, and the family had been without heat for two nights.”

title: The Past Perfect Tense: The Past Before the Past
text:
Knowledge Check
1. Choose the correct sentence: A) When I arrived, they already ate. B) When I arrived, they had already eaten.
2. Convert to reported speech: “I have finished,” he said. A) He said he has finished. B) He said he had finished.
3. Which conditional uses the past perfect? A) The second conditional B) The third conditional

Answer Key

B. The earlier completed action (eaten) precedes the later past event (arrived), so it takes the past perfect.
B. Reported speech shifts the present perfect back to the past perfect.
B. The third conditional (If I had known, I would have…) describes an unreal past.
